paragraphs.text: וְאֵ֙לֶּה֙ תּוֹלְדֹ֣ת בְּנֵי־נֹ֔חַ שֵׁ֖ם חָ֣ם וָיָ֑פֶת וַיִּוָּלְד֥וּ לָהֶ֛ם בָּנִ֖ים אַחַ֥ר הַמַּבּֽוּל׃

i18n.en: These are the begettings of the sons of Noah — Shem, Ham, and Yapheth; sons were born to them after the deluge.

paragraphs.commentary: **The toledot formula resumes.** This is the fourth *toledot* in Genesis (after 2:4 of the skies and the land, 5:1 of Adam, 6:9 of Noah), and the first to organize an ethnographic catalogue rather than a personal genealogy. The chapter's structure mirrors the Flood-clean-slate: after the Flood, the human family branches into the three lines that will populate the post-Flood world. *Acharei ha-mabbul* — *after the deluge* — names the chronological frame: everything in this chapter unfolds in the new era.

paragraphs.text: בְּנֵ֣י יֶ֔פֶת גֹּ֣מֶר וּמָג֔וֹג וּמָדַ֖י וְיָוָ֣ן וְתֻבָ֑ל וּמֶ֖שֶׁךְ וְתִירָֽס׃

i18n.en: The sons of Yapheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Yavan, Tuval, Meshech, and Tiras.

paragraphs.commentary: **The Japhethite line — the peoples of the northern and western rim.** The names map onto the Mediterranean and Black Sea horizon of the Hebrew Bible's geographic imagination: *Gomer* with the Cimmerians (Akkadian *Gimirrai*); *Magog* a region north of the Caucasus (Ezek 38–39's eschatological adversary); *Madai* the Medes (Iran); *Yavan* the Greeks (Ionia); *Tuval* and *Meshech* in eastern Anatolia (Tabal and Mushki in Assyrian sources); *Tiras* possibly the Tyrsenoi (Etruscans) or Thracians. The chapter places the Japhethites in the lands that Israel later encounters as trade partners, distant rivals, or apocalyptic threats — but rarely as direct neighbors.

paragraphs.text: וּבְנֵ֖י גֹּ֑מֶר אַשְׁכֲּנַ֥ז וְרִיפַ֖ת וְתֹגַרְמָֽה׃

i18n.en: The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah.

paragraphs.text: וּבְנֵ֥י יָוָ֖ן אֱלִישָׁ֣ה וְתַרְשִׁ֑ישׁ כִּתִּ֖ים וְדֹדָנִֽים׃

i18n.en: The sons of Yavan: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim.

paragraphs.commentary: **Greek-world toponyms.** *Elishah* is generally identified with Cyprus (Alashiya in Late Bronze Age sources). *Tarshish* is the Hebrew Bible's far-western trading horizon — variously identified with Tartessos (southern Spain), Sardinia, or a generic 'farthest west' label. *Kittim* is Cyprus or coastal Greece in its earliest usage, later extended to refer to Romans and other western powers in later prophetic and Qumran literature. *Dodanim* is read as *Rodanim* in some manuscripts (Rhodes); the *daleth/resh* swap is a common scribal variant in Hebrew.

paragraphs.text: מֵ֠אֵלֶּה נִפְרְד֞וּ אִיֵּ֤י הַגּוֹיִם֙ בְּאַרְצֹתָ֔ם אִ֖ישׁ לִלְשֹׁנ֑וֹ לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתָ֖ם בְּגוֹיֵהֶֽם׃

i18n.en: From these the coastlands of the nations were separated into their lands, each by his tongue, by their families, in their nations.

paragraphs.commentary: **The summary formula for the Japhethite branch.** *Iyei ha-goyim* — *coastlands of the nations* — names the Japhethites as the maritime, language-distinct peoples of the rim. The formula has four dimensions: *lands* (geographic), *tongues* (linguistic), *families* (kinship), *nations* (political). The same four dimensions recur in the summary formulae for the Hamite line (v20) and the Shemite line (v31). The fact that the language-distinction is already in place here, *before* the Babel narrative of chapter 11, is one of the chapter's structural seams: the Table of Nations presents linguistic diversity as a present reality; chapter 11 explains its origin. The two are different sources stitched together; the redactor preserved both. The result is a chapter that says *each by his tongue* before the chapter that says how they came to have different tongues.

paragraphs.text: וּבְנֵ֖י חָ֑ם כּ֥וּשׁ וּמִצְרַ֖יִם וּפ֥וּט וּכְנָֽעַן׃

i18n.en: The sons of Ham: Kush, Mitsrayim, Put, and Canaan.

paragraphs.commentary: **The Hamite line — the southern and southwestern peoples.** *Kush* is the Nile-valley region south of Egypt (Nubia / modern Sudan); *Mitsrayim* is the dual-form name for Egypt (literally 'the two Mitsrayims' — Upper and Lower Egypt, the dual reflecting the political duality of the Egyptian state in the Hebrew Bible's view); *Put* is Libya or the eastern African coast; *Canaan* is the land Israel will later occupy. The Hamites are framed as the peoples Israel will encounter on its southern borders and within its eventual territory.

paragraphs.text: וּבְנֵ֣י כ֔וּשׁ סְבָא֙ וַֽחֲוִילָ֔ה וְסַבְתָּ֥ה וְרַעְמָ֖ה וְסַבְתְּכָ֑א וּבְנֵ֥י רַעְמָ֖ה שְׁבָ֥א וּדְדָֽן׃

i18n.en: The sons of Kush: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabtecha; and the sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan.

paragraphs.text: וְכ֖וּשׁ יָלַ֣ד אֶת־נִמְרֹ֑ד ה֣וּא הֵחֵ֔ל לִֽהְי֥וֹת גִּבֹּ֖ר בָּאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: And Kush fathered Nimrod — he was the first to be a mighty one in the land.

paragraphs.commentary: **The Nimrod parenthesis opens.** The chapter pauses its enumeration to introduce a single named figure across five verses (v8–12). *Hu hechel lihyot gibbor ba-aretz* — *he was the first to be a mighty one in the land* — uses the same noun גִּבּוֹר *gibbor* that named the antediluvian *gibborim anshei ha-shem* of 6:4 (the offspring of the *bnei ha-elohim* with the daughters of the human). The post-Flood world has its first *gibbor*, and the chapter names him: Nimrod. The verbal echo across 6:4 and 10:8 is unmistakable — the chapter is asserting that the *gibbor*-class did not end with the Flood. How that survives the wipe-out of 7:23 is the same problem the Nephilim raise in Numbers 13:33, and the chapter does not resolve it.

paragraphs.text: הֽוּא־הָיָ֥ה גִבֹּֽר־צַ֖יִד לִפְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה עַל־כֵּן֙ יֵֽאָמַ֔ר כְּנִמְרֹ֛ד גִּבּ֥וֹר צַ֖יִד לִפְנֵ֥י יְהוָֽה׃

i18n.en: He was a mighty hunter before YHWH; therefore it is said: 'Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before YHWH.'

paragraphs.commentary: **A proverb embedded in the narrative.** The chapter cites a popular saying — *like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before YHWH* — as already in circulation in the period the chapter is composed. The text is reporting a folk-tradition about Nimrod, not constructing one. // The preposition לִפְנֵי *lifnei* ('before, in the presence of') is grammatically neutral — it can mean 'in the favor of' (positive), 'in defiance of' (adversarial), or simply 'in the sight of' (witnessed by). Jewish tradition has read it as adversarial (Nimrod the rebel-against-YHWH, builder of Babel); Christian tradition has often read it as positive (Nimrod the divinely-empowered hunter). The Hebrew settles neither. The chapter places Nimrod *visible to YHWH* without taking sides on the relationship's polarity. // *Tzayid* — *hunter* — names a specialized warrior-class skill. In ANE iconography, royal lion-hunting was the signature image of kingship (Assyrian palace reliefs; the Standard of Ur). Nimrod the *gibbor-tzayid* is the Hebrew Bible's compressed image of the founder-king.

paragraphs.text: וַתְּהִ֨י רֵאשִׁ֤ית מַמְלַכְתּוֹ֙ בָּבֶ֔ל וְאֶ֖רֶךְ וְאַכַּ֣ד וְכַלְנֵ֑ה בְּאֶ֖רֶץ שִׁנְעָֽר׃

i18n.en: The beginning of his kingdom was Babel, and Erech, and Akkad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar.

paragraphs.commentary: **The founding of Mesopotamian civilization, named.** The chapter attributes the four foundational southern-Mesopotamian cities to a single founder — Nimrod. *Babel* (Bavel in Hebrew) — the future Babylon, whose ziggurat will be the subject of chapter 11. *Erech* — Sumerian Uruk, the great walled city of the third-millennium-BCE Sumerian world; archaeologically the largest city of its era. *Akkad* — the capital of Sargon's third-millennium empire, the first political entity to project unified rule across all of Mesopotamia; its location is archaeologically unknown but textually well-attested. *Calneh* — uncertain identification; possibly Nippur (the Sumerian religious center) or an unidentified site. // *Eretz Shinar* — *the land of Shinar* — is the chapter's standard Hebrew term for the alluvial plain of southern Mesopotamia (Sumer + Akkad). It returns in 11:2 as the location of Babel-tower construction, in 14:1 (Amraphel king of Shinar), and in later prophetic literature (Isa 11:11, Zech 5:11, Dan 1:2) where it carries an exilic register. // The Wheel of Heaven lens reads this verse with attention: the chapter is naming Mesopotamia as the cradle of post-Flood civilization, attributing the founding to a *gibbor* whose lineage traces (via Cush) to Ham. The first city-founder of the post-Flood world is, on the Hebrew's terms, a *mighty one* in the same vocabulary as the antediluvian *gibborim anshei ha-shem*. The connection between human technological-political ambition and the *gibbor*-class is being drawn at the chapter's textual surface.

paragraphs.text: מִן־הָאָ֥רֶץ הַהִ֖וא יָצָ֣א אַשּׁ֑וּר וַיִּ֙בֶן֙ אֶת־נִ֣ינְוֵ֔ה וְאֶת־רְחֹבֹ֥ת עִ֖יר וְאֶת־כָּֽלַח׃

i18n.en: From that land Asshur went out, and built Nineveh, and Rehoboth-Ir, and Calah.

paragraphs.commentary: **The Mesopotamian-civilization founding extends north.** The verse is grammatically ambiguous about who *Asshur* is: (a) Asshur the *person* (a son of Shem, named in v22) went out from Shinar and founded the northern Mesopotamian cities, OR (b) reading the same consonants as a verbal phrase, *Nimrod* went out to *Assyria* and built those cities (this is the marginal Jewish reading: 'from that land *he* went out *to Assyria*'). The plain reading is (a), with Asshur the founder of northern Mesopotamian civilization paralleling Nimrod's founding of southern Mesopotamian civilization. // *Nineveh* is the future Assyrian capital (modern Mosul region). *Rehoboth-Ir* (literally 'broad-places city') and *Calah* (Kalhu, modern Nimrud — named for Nimrod in traditional etymology) are the other major Assyrian cities. The chapter is compressing the entire ANE city-founding tradition into two figures: Nimrod for the south, Asshur for the north.

paragraphs.text: וְֽאֶת־רֶ֔סֶן בֵּ֥ין נִֽינְוֵ֖ה וּבֵ֣ין כָּ֑לַח הִ֖וא הָעִ֥יר הַגְּדֹלָֽה׃

i18n.en: And Resen, between Nineveh and Calah — that is the great city.

paragraphs.commentary: ***Ha-ir ha-gedolah*** — *the great city*. The phrase has a sticky referent: grammatically it can attach to *Resen* (the immediately preceding city) or to *Calah*, or it can be read as a summary descriptor of the whole Nineveh-Rehoboth-Calah-Resen complex (the 'great city' as the larger metropolitan area). The phrase echoes Jonah 1:2, 3:2, 4:11, where *the great city* is unambiguously Nineveh. The Genesis chapter probably uses the phrase in the larger-complex sense; Jonah will later use it to name Nineveh specifically. The Nimrod parenthesis closes here.

paragraphs.text: וּמִצְרַ֡יִם יָלַ֞ד אֶת־לוּדִ֧ים וְאֶת־עֲנָמִ֛ים וְאֶת־לְהָבִ֖ים וְאֶת־נַפְתֻּחִֽים׃

i18n.en: Mitsrayim fathered the Ludim, the Anamim, the Lehabim, and the Naphtuhim.

paragraphs.text: וְֽאֶת־פַּתְרֻסִ֞ים וְאֶת־כַּסְלֻחִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֨ר יָצְא֥וּ מִשָּׁ֛ם פְּלִשְׁתִּ֖ים וְאֶת־כַּפְתֹּרִֽים׃

i18n.en: and the Patrusim, and the Casluhim — from whom the Pelishtim went out — and the Caphtorim.

paragraphs.commentary: **The Philistines come from where?** The parenthesis אֲשֶׁר יָצְאוּ מִשָּׁם פְּלִשְׁתִּים — *from whom the Pelishtim went out* — places the Philistines as descendants of the *Casluhim*. But the prophetic tradition (Jer 47:4, Amos 9:7) and the consensus modern reading (matching Egyptian and Aegean archaeological evidence) trace the Philistines from *Caphtor* (Crete / the Aegean), not from the Casluhim. The parenthesis may be a scribal misplacement: it should attach to the Caphtorim that immediately follow. The textual problem is well-attested in the manuscript tradition. // Either way, the chapter is locating the Philistines (the Iron Age I newcomers who would dominate Israel's south-coast throughout the Judges and early monarchy period) within the Hamite-Egyptian sphere — which is geographically and culturally accurate to the Sea-Peoples-origin model that contemporary archaeology supports.

paragraphs.text: וּכְנַ֗עַן יָלַ֛ד אֶת־צִידֹ֥ן בְּכֹר֖וֹ וְאֶת־חֵֽת׃

i18n.en: Canaan fathered Sidon his firstborn, and Heth.

paragraphs.commentary: **The Canaanite line.** *Tsidon* (Sidon) is the Phoenician city on the Lebanese coast — the chapter names it as Canaan's firstborn, locating the Phoenician civilization as the senior Canaanite descendant. *Cheth* is the Hittites — though the biblical Hittites are likely a distinct group (Anatolian sub-population residing in Canaan) from the Anatolian Hittite Empire.

paragraphs.text: וְאֶת־הַיְבוּסִי֙ וְאֶת־הָ֣אֱמֹרִ֔י וְאֵ֖ת הַגִּרְגָּשִֽׁי׃

i18n.en: and the Jebusite, the Amorite, and the Girgashite,

paragraphs.text: וְאֶת־הַֽחִוִּ֥י וְאֶת־הַֽעַרְקִ֖י וְאֶת־הַסִּינִֽי׃

i18n.en: and the Hivite, the Arkite, and the Sinite,

paragraphs.text: וְאֶת־הָֽאַרְוָדִ֥י וְאֶת־הַצְּמָרִ֖י וְאֶת־הַֽחֲמָתִ֑י וְאַחַ֣ר נָפֹ֔צוּ מִשְׁפְּח֖וֹת הַֽכְּנַעֲנִֽי׃

i18n.en: and the Arvadite, the Zemarite, and the Hamathite. Afterward the families of the Canaanite were scattered.

paragraphs.commentary: *Naphotzu* — *they were scattered*. The verb is the same as in 11:8–9 (YHWH scattered the people from Babel) and in 9:19 (the scattering from Noah's sons). The Canaanite peoples are placed by the chapter as a scattered cluster, with no single political center — the geographic spread to be detailed in v19.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְהִ֞י גְּב֤וּל הַֽכְּנַעֲנִי֙ מִצִּידֹ֔ן בֹּאֲכָ֥ה גְרָ֖רָה עַד־עַזָּ֑ה בֹּאֲכָ֞ה סְדֹ֧מָה וַעֲמֹרָ֛ה וְאַדְמָ֥ה וּצְבֹיִ֖ם עַד־לָֽשַׁע׃

i18n.en: The territory of the Canaanite extended from Sidon, in the direction of Gerar, as far as Gaza, in the direction of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboim, as far as Lasha.

paragraphs.commentary: **The geography of Canaan, prospectively.** The chapter is sketching the area Israel will later occupy as a single political-ethnographic zone, defining its boundaries by the major coastal city (Sidon in the north), the southern coastal-plain cities (Gerar and Gaza), the cities of the plain (Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboim — destroyed in Gen 19), and an eastern limit (Lasha, location uncertain). The verse is one of the chapter's clearer cases where the post-Flood ethnographic frame includes information that only makes sense in light of later narrative — the chapter is composed in awareness of Sodom-Gomorrah's later destruction and Israel's later occupation.

paragraphs.text: אֵ֣לֶּה בְנֵי־חָ֔ם לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתָ֖ם לִלְשֹֽׁנֹתָ֑ם בְּאַרְצֹתָ֖ם בְּגוֹיֵהֶֽם׃

i18n.en: These are the sons of Ham, by their families, by their tongues, in their lands, in their nations.

paragraphs.text: וּלְשֵׁ֥ם יֻלַּ֖ד גַּם־ה֑וּא אֲבִי֙ כָּל־בְּנֵי־עֵ֔בֶר אֲחִ֖י יֶ֥פֶת הַגָּדֽוֹל׃

i18n.en: To Shem also there were born — he the father of all the sons of Eber, the elder brother of Yapheth.

paragraphs.commentary: **Shem is identified as *the father of all the sons of Eber*.** The verse anticipates v24–25, where Eber appears as Shem's great-grandson. The early identification flags Eber's prospective importance: עֵבֶר *Eber* is the eponymous ancestor of the *Ivri* (Hebrew) people — the etymology is widely (though not universally) accepted in modern scholarship. The chapter is opening the Shemite branch by naming, four generations ahead, the figure from whom Israel's own self-designation will derive. // *Achi Yepheth ha-gadol* — *the elder brother of Yapheth*. The Hebrew grammar is ambiguous about whether *ha-gadol* (the elder/great) modifies *Yepheth* (making Yapheth the elder brother) or *Shem* (making Shem the elder); the standard reading is the former. The chapter is positioning Yapheth as the eldest of Noah's three sons, even though the listing order (Shem, Ham, Yapheth) has placed Shem first throughout. The ordering is by *prominence* (Shem-line is Israel's), not by birth order.

paragraphs.text: בְּנֵ֥י שֵׁ֖ם עֵילָ֣ם וְאַשּׁ֑וּר וְאַרְפַּכְשַׁ֖ד וְל֥וּד וַֽאֲרָֽם׃

i18n.en: The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, and Aram.

paragraphs.commentary: **The Shemite line — the peoples of the eastern and northeastern arc.** *Elam* is the powerful eastern neighbor of Mesopotamia (southwestern Iran; the capital Susa). *Asshur* is the Assyrian people (the name is identical to the founder of v11 — possibly a doublet, possibly two distinct figures sharing the name). *Arpachshad* is the ancestor through whom the line will pass to Eber, Peleg, and ultimately Abraham. *Lud* is variously identified (Lydia in Anatolia, or a Semitic Lud). *Aram* is the Aramean peoples of upper Mesopotamia and Syria — Israel's later northern cousins in language and culture.

paragraphs.text: וּבְנֵ֖י אֲרָ֑ם ע֥וּץ וְח֖וּל וְגֶ֥תֶר וָמַֽשׁ׃

i18n.en: The sons of Aram: Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash.

paragraphs.commentary: *Uz* is the homeland of Job (Job 1:1, 'in the land of Uz'). The Aramean placement of Uz is one of the data-points by which Job is read as a non-Israelite text the Hebrew Bible nevertheless preserved as canonical.

paragraphs.text: וְאַרְפַּכְשַׁ֖ד יָלַ֣ד אֶת־שָׁ֑לַח וְשֶׁ֖לַח יָלַ֥ד אֶת־עֵֽבֶר׃

i18n.en: Arpachshad fathered Shelach, and Shelach fathered Eber.

paragraphs.text: וּלְעֵ֥בֶר יֻלַּ֖ד שְׁנֵ֣י בָנִ֑ים שֵׁ֣ם הָֽאֶחָ֞ד פֶּ֗לֶג כִּ֤י בְיָמָיו֙ נִפְלְגָ֣ה הָאָ֔רֶץ וְשֵׁ֥ם אָחִ֖יו יָקְטָֽן׃

i18n.en: To Eber were born two sons; the name of the one was Peleg, for in his days the land was divided; and his brother's name was Yoqtan.

paragraphs.commentary: **The first explicit dating-by-event in Genesis 10.** *Peleg* — פֶּלֶג — is from the root פלג *palag* 'to divide, split'. The chapter glosses the name etiologically: *ki b'yamav niflega ha-aretz* — *for in his days the land was divided*. // What division? Three readings: // (1) **The linguistic division of Babel** (Gen 11). The chapter places Peleg in the genealogy just before the Babel narrative; the etiology pairs his name with the scattering-of-languages event. This is the standard ancient and modern interpretation. // (2) **A geological / continental division** — the reading favored by some modern creationist and ancient-astronaut traditions: that the splitting of continents (sometimes proposed as a post-Flood event) is what is meant. There is no support for this reading in the Hebrew lexicon or in the chapter's own self-frame. // (3) **A political-territorial division** — the division of post-Flood lands among the descendants of Noah, the very catalogue the chapter is providing. The verb is used elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible for the division of inherited land (Job 38:25). // The chapter does not specify which division is meant. The most contextually defensible reading is (1), the linguistic-political scattering; (3) is supplementary. (2) is interpretive and reads back from later cosmological frames. The translation preserves the bare 'the land was divided' and lets the commentary surface the spectrum.

paragraphs.text: וְיָקְטָ֣ן יָלַ֔ד אֶת־אַלְמוֹדָ֖ד וְאֶת־שָׁ֑לֶף וְאֶת־חֲצַרְמָ֖וֶת וְאֶת־יָֽרַח׃

i18n.en: Yoqtan fathered Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, and Yerach.

paragraphs.text: וְאֶת־הֲדוֹרָ֥ם וְאֶת־אוּזָ֖ל וְאֶת־דִּקְלָֽה׃

i18n.en: Hadoram, Uzal, and Diqlah,

paragraphs.text: וְאֶת־עוֹבָ֥ל וְאֶת־אֲבִֽימָאֵ֖ל וְאֶת־שְׁבָֽא׃

i18n.en: Obal, Abimael, and Sheba,

paragraphs.text: וְאֶת־אוֹפִ֥ר וְאֶת־חֲוִילָ֖ה וְאֶת־יוֹבָ֑ב כָּל־אֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֥י יָקְטָֽן׃

i18n.en: Ophir, Havilah, and Yobab — all these were the sons of Yoqtan.

paragraphs.commentary: **The Yoqtanite line is the Arabian-peninsula branch.** Several of the names map onto South Arabian and Yemenite locations — *Hazarmaveth* (v26) is the Hadramawt region of Yemen; *Sheba* is the famous spice-trade kingdom (Saba); *Ophir* is the proverbial Hebrew Bible source of gold (1 Kgs 9:28, 10:11). The Shemite line forks at Eber into two branches: Peleg's line carries forward toward Abraham; Yoqtan's line populates Arabia.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְהִ֥י מוֹשָׁבָ֖ם מִמֵּשָׁ֑א בֹּאֲכָ֥ה סְפָ֖רָה הַ֥ר הַקֶּֽדֶם׃

i18n.en: Their dwelling extended from Mesha in the direction of Sephar — the mountain of the east.

paragraphs.text: אֵ֣לֶּה בְנֵי־שֵׁ֔ם לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתָ֖ם לִלְשֹׁנֹתָ֑ם בְּאַרְצֹתָ֖ם לְגוֹיֵהֶֽם׃

i18n.en: These are the sons of Shem, by their families, by their tongues, in their lands, by their nations.

paragraphs.text: אֵ֣לֶּה מִשְׁפְּחֹ֧ת בְּנֵי־נֹ֛חַ לְתוֹלְדֹתָ֖ם בְּגוֹיֵהֶ֑ם וּמֵאֵ֜לֶּה נִפְרְד֧וּ הַגּוֹיִ֛ם בָּאָ֖רֶץ אַחַ֥ר הַמַּבּֽוּל׃

i18n.en: These are the families of the sons of Noah, by their begettings, in their nations; and from these the nations were separated on the land after the deluge.

paragraphs.commentary: **The closing summary frames the whole chapter as a single ethnographic act.** *Mishpechot bnei Noach l'toledotam b'goyehem* — *the families of the sons of Noah, by their begettings, in their nations*. The four organizing dimensions of the chapter (family, lineage, geography, polity) are listed in the closing verse, sealing the catalogue. // The verb *niphredu* — *were separated* — runs through the chapter: at v5 (the Japhethite coastlands), implicit in v18 (the Canaanites *naphotzu* scattered), and now in v32 as the universal closing claim. The chapter's keyword is *separation* — the post-Flood world is the *separated* world. Babel in chapter 11 will explain why.
